subject: history
displayName: KS3 History — The British Empire & Colonialism
subtitle: The growth of the British Empire, its methods of control, and its long-term consequences.

data.targetWord: a group of territories controlled by one ruler, state or country, often through military, economic or political power

examples.en-GB: The British Empire at its height controlled territories across every continent, from Canada to India to Australia.

data.targetWord: a territory controlled by another country, often far away, where the ruling power exercises political, military or economic authority

examples.en-GB: Jamaica was a British colony where plantation owners relied on enslaved African labour to produce sugar.

data.targetWord: the system of taking control of other lands and peoples, often for settlement, profit, power or resources, involving unequal political relationships

examples.en-GB: Colonialism changed land ownership, legal systems and economies across the territories Britain controlled.

data.targetWord: the policy of expanding a country's power and influence, sometimes through direct colonies and sometimes through economic or political pressure

examples.en-GB: British imperialism involved not only direct rule but also informal empire through trade, loans and naval pressure.

data.targetWord: a powerful British trading company founded in 1600 that gained political and military control over large parts of India before direct Crown rule began in 1858

examples.en-GB: The East India Company's victory at the Battle of Plassey in 1757 gave it major power over Bengal and its tax revenues.

data.targetWord: a colony where large numbers of people from the ruling country moved to live permanently, often taking land from indigenous peoples

examples.en-GB: Australia was a settler colony where British colonisation began in 1788 and had devastating effects on Aboriginal peoples.

data.targetWord: actions taken by colonised peoples to oppose imperial control, including protest, refusal, rebellion, legal challenge, cultural survival and warfare

examples.en-GB: The Indian Rebellion of 1857 was a major example of resistance against East India Company rule, involving sepoys and many other groups.

data.targetWord: influence over a country through trade, loans, diplomacy or military pressure, without direct colonial rule

examples.en-GB: Britain exercised informal empire over parts of Latin America by controlling trade and lending money to local governments.

data.targetWord: strength at sea, including warships, ports and the ability to protect trade routes and project military force across long distances

examples.en-GB: British naval power allowed it to protect merchant shipping, seize territories and maintain control of key sea routes like Gibraltar.

data.targetWord: using people, land or resources unfairly for someone else's benefit, often without fair compensation or consent

examples.en-GB: The exploitation of colonised peoples' labour and land created wealth for British merchants and investors.

data.targetWord: an Indian soldier employed by the East India Company to serve in its armies in India

examples.en-GB: Sepoy soldiers began the Indian Rebellion of 1857, which then spread to include rulers, peasants and townspeople across northern India.

data.targetWord: the false belief that some groups of people are superior or inferior because of supposed racial differences, used to justify empire, enslavement and unequal rights

examples.en-GB: Racist ideas claiming that European civilisation was superior were used to justify British rule over colonised peoples.

data.targetWord: the long-term effects of past events, decisions or systems on the present, including effects on borders, wealth, culture, migration and inequality

examples.en-GB: The legacy of the British Empire is still debated today, including discussions about statues, museum objects and the wealth it created.

data.targetWord: the defeat of the Nawab of Bengal by the East India Company, giving the Company major influence over Bengal's territory and tax revenues

examples.en-GB: The Battle of Plassey in 1757 marked a turning point after which the East India Company shifted from trading company to territorial power in India.

data.targetWord: a major uprising against East India Company rule in India, beginning among sepoys and spreading to include various other groups before being violently suppressed

examples.en-GB: The Indian Rebellion of 1857 shocked Britain and led to the end of East India Company rule; the British Crown took direct control of India in 1858.

data.targetWord: a meeting of European powers that set rules for claiming African territory, without proper representation of African rulers or peoples

examples.en-GB: The Berlin Conference of 1884-85 showed how European powers divided Africa among themselves without consulting African peoples.

data.targetWord: a person who travels to spread a religion; in the British Empire, Christian missionaries also set up schools and hospitals but sometimes undermined local cultures

examples.en-GB: Missionaries in colonial Africa set up schools that spread Christianity and English literacy but also challenged local beliefs and authority.

data.targetWord: the period of direct British Crown rule over India from 1858 to 1947, following the abolition of East India Company control after the 1857 Rebellion

examples.en-GB: During the British Raj, India was often called the 'jewel in the crown' of the British Empire because of its wealth, soldiers and strategic importance.

data.targetWord: the return of objects, artworks or human remains to the communities or countries from which they were taken, often debated in the context of colonial collections

examples.en-GB: Debates about restitution concern whether museums in Britain should return objects acquired from colonised countries during the imperial period.

data.targetWord: a legal idea meaning 'empty land', used by Britain to justify claiming Australia as if it belonged to no one, ignoring Aboriginal peoples' long presence and rights

examples.en-GB: The idea of terra nullius was used to dismiss Aboriginal Australians' rights to their land, despite thousands of years of Indigenous occupation.

data.targetWord: a place or group of buyers to whom goods can be sold; overseas markets were important for British manufacturers to sell their products

examples.en-GB: India provided a large market for British manufactured cotton cloth, which undercut local Indian weavers.

data.targetWord: information about where a source comes from, who made it, when, why and for whom, which is essential when evaluating evidence about empire

examples.en-GB: A colonial advertisement's provenance tells us it was made to sell goods and build positive images of empire, not to document colonial suffering.

data.targetWord: a treaty signed in 1840 between the British Crown and many Maori chiefs in New Zealand, which later caused disputes because of differences between the English and Maori versions

examples.en-GB: The Treaty of Waitangi was meant to agree the terms of British settlement in New Zealand, but disputes over its meaning led to conflict over land and sovereignty.

data.targetWord: an economic system based on large farms growing a single export crop such as sugar or cotton, dependent on enslaved or forced labour

examples.en-GB: Caribbean colonies operated plantation economies producing sugar through enslaved African labour, generating profits for British merchants.

data.targetWord: the movement of people from one place to another; empire caused migration in multiple directions — settlers moved to colonies, and people from colonies also came to Britain

examples.en-GB: Empire caused migration both ways: British settlers moved to Australia and Canada, while sailors, students and workers from colonies travelled to Britain.

data.sentence: A territory controlled by another country, often far away, is called a ____.
The East India Company gained major power over Bengal after its victory at the Battle of ____ in 1757.
In 1858, after the Indian Rebellion, the British ____ took direct control of India, ending Company rule.
Queen Victoria was declared ____ of India in 1876, symbolising the empire's importance.
Indian soldiers employed by the East India Company were called ____.
The legal idea that Australia was 'empty land', ignoring Aboriginal peoples' rights, was called ____ nullius.
The ____ Conference of 1884-85 was where European powers agreed rules for claiming African territory.
British influence over a country through trade and finance without direct rule is called ____ empire.
The return of objects from colonial collections to their countries of origin is called ____.
Ports such as Liverpool and ____ grew wealthy through imperial trade in sugar, tobacco and cotton.
A colony where large numbers of settlers from Britain moved to live permanently, often displacing indigenous peoples, is called a ____ colony.
False ideas claiming one group of people is naturally superior because of their race are called ____.
The treaty signed in 1840 between Britain and Maori chiefs in New Zealand was called the Treaty of ____.
India was sometimes called the 'jewel in the ____' of the British Empire because of its wealth and strategic importance.
Long-term effects of the British Empire on modern borders, culture and inequality are called its ____.
The period of direct British Crown rule over India from 1858 to 1947 is known as the British ____.

data.title: Put these key events in the history of the British Empire in chronological order.
items: Battle of Plassey — Company gains power in Bengal (1757)
British Crown takes direct control of India (1858)
Queen Victoria declared Empress of India (1876)

data.title: Arrange these events relating to Britain and India in chronological order.
items: East India Company founded to trade in Asia (1600)
Company defeats the Nawab of Bengal at Plassey (1757)
Company governs India with its own armies and tax collection
Sepoys and others rebel against Company rule (1857)
British Crown ends Company rule and governs India directly (1858)
Queen Victoria becomes Empress of India (1876)

data.title: Arrange this consequence chain of British imperial expansion in logical order.
items: British control expands through trade, war and treaties
Land and laws change in colonised territories
Taxes and labour demands increase for colonised peoples
Local rulers and communities lose power
Long-term debates about memory and legacy continue

data.title: Sort each reason for building the British Empire into the correct category of motive.

pairs.text: merchants wanted raw materials like cotton, tea and sugar
factories needed markets to sell British manufactured goods
investors wanted opportunities in colonial railways and mines
Britain wanted to compete with France and Spain for global power
politicians wanted prestige and influence in international affairs
naval bases like Gibraltar and Singapore controlled sea routes
controlling Cape Town allowed ships to reach India more safely
missionaries wanted to spread Christianity to colonised peoples
racist ideas claimed British rule was superior and civilising

data.title: Sort each statement into whether it describes an impact on Britain or an impact on colonised peoples.

pairs.text: tea, sugar and cotton clothing became part of everyday British life
ports like Liverpool and Bristol grew through imperial trade
museums collected objects from around the empire
British identity became linked to naval power and empire
indigenous peoples often lost their land to settlers
local rulers lost sovereignty to British officials or Company control
missionary schools promoted Christianity and undermined local beliefs
colonial railways were built to move export goods rather than serve local needs
